newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Powerless aid agencies urge Zaire military action.
newsitem.headline: Powerless aid agencies urge Zaire military action.

text.p: Pressure grew on Western powers on Friday to save one million refugees on the run in east Zaire as aid agencies admitted their impotence and the International Committee of the Red Cross called for military intervention.

Amid reports of refugees disappearing in inaccessible jungles and some dying on lava fields near volcanoes in eastern Zaire's north Kivu region, the head of the Geneva-based ICRC said a Western military intervention was the only way out.

"There is no other option," Cornelio Sommaruga told Reuters after a news conference on the humanitarian crisis triggered by a complex multi-sided war in eastern Zaire which has cut off more than one million Rwandan refugees from the outside world.
On Thursday, Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said a neutral force should be sent by the West to set up safe routes to deliver aid through fighting.

Weeks of hand-wringing by governments have so far produced no international consensus on what can be done for the refugees, trapped in a region where the United States and other major Western powers have little strategic or economic interest.

France and Spain say they could send 1,000 men each as part of a 5,000-men force with U.N. approval. But Rwanda's new Tutsi rulers are mistrustful of France, which was a key military ally of the former extremist Hutu leaders who led 1994's genocide.
Sommaruga, speaking at the news conference, appealed to the U.N. Security Council to urgently take necessary measures.
"There is an extreme urgency. The victims cannot wait any longer. I'd like to recall the responsabilities of the international community. The ICRC is expecting action," he said.
"It's up to the international community to make the choice and see to it that humanitarian agencies are able to act."
U.N. relief agencies expressed bitterness at being unable to act as stocks of aid piled up around east Africa to feed and shelter the victims only when it is safe to do so.
"Our impotence to react to this catastrophic situation must be recognised," the U.N. children's agency spokeswoman Marie Heuze told a briefing.
The United Nations Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA) reported an estimated 175,000 refugees who fled camps in Goma were heading west towards lava fields.
Refugees were already dying on the fields, which emit dangerous gases, and had no water or food. Others were heading for the bush and jungles, according to DHA.
Competing armed groups of Zairean soldiers from various divisions and Rwandan Hutu militiamen were roaming the area and fleeing Zairean troops were looting their way towards Kisangani town, it said.
The International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it feared an outbreak of cholera epidemics in eastern Zaire which could claim thousands of lives.
A cholera outbreak in Goma after 1994's exodus of Rwandan Hutu refugees claimed at least 30,000 lives.
"There is an enormous risk of cholera. That would be a catastrophe," Piero Calvi-Parisetti, IFRC head for Africa's troubled Great Lakes region, told a news conference in Geneva.
Ruth Marshall, spokeswoman for the U.N. refugee agency, said Western states had not responded to UNHCR's appeal on October 29 for U.S. satellite pictures to trace the refugees.
"No one has given us any satellite photographs," she said. "I don't think the (U.S.) government has given us any. We don't have any in our house. It would help if we had."
